strengths: The paper addresses a useful and underexplored problem: generating 3D shapes from sequential VR sketches while retaining stroke and point order.

The proposed dataset is potentially valuable, combining 20,838 automatically generated pairs with 900 human-drawn pairs across four categories; preserving temporal annotations distinguishes it from existing public VR-sketch datasets.
The method is technically plausible and clearly motivated: Fourier-encoded spatial and sequence features are processed by a lightweight transformer and used to condition a latent 3D diffusion model.

Reported gains are substantial on both 3DVRChair and the proposed benchmark. The zero-shot chair ablation also provides evidence that sequence-related embeddings help: removing them reduces F-score from 56.8 to 48.9 and increases CD from 5.1 to 7.1.

The paper includes useful analyses of synthetic pretraining, alternative sketch representations, partial inputs, inference cost, and qualitative topology preservation. The figures are generally clear and the main pipeline is easy to follow.
weaknesses: A material concern is that the dataset split is insufficiently specified. The paper does not report the number of unique source shapes, sketches per shape, or whether ShapeNet identities are disjoint across synthetic training, real fine-tuning, and real evaluation. If an evaluation target—or a closely duplicated ShapeNet model—also generated a synthetic training sketch, the large gains could partly reflect shape memorization. Participant-disjointness is likewise unspecified.

The real sketches are drawn directly over reference meshes and projected to their surfaces. This produces unusually accurate traces rather than the noisy, independently conceived sketches motivating the work. Consequently, the experiments do not establish performance for ordinary free-space VR ideation. Table 1 cannot validate the benefit of snapping because it compares different datasets, categories, and collection protocols rather than snapped and unsnapped sketches under controlled conditions.

The central claim that temporal order is responsible for the improvement is not isolated convincingly. The only ordering ablation jointly removes stroke and within-stroke index embeddings, thereby changing both segmentation/position information at once. There is no controlled permutation test—such as shuffling stroke order or reversing points while preserving all tokens—and the training augmentation itself swaps 20% of strokes. Thus, the evidence shows that the positional features are useful, but not which ordering signal matters or whether human drawing order is superior to an arbitrary consistent ordering.

Several experimental inconsistencies weaken confidence in the evidence. Figure 5 reports up to 200 real training samples per category, although the described fine-tuning set contains only 100 samples for each non-chair category. The exact subset, sampling protocol, repetitions, and uncertainty are not reported. Diffusion results likewise lack evaluation across random seeds or clarification of whether one or multiple generated samples are used per sketch.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate. The paper alternately describes the U-Net as predicting a denoised latent and optimizing latent reconstruction, while the diagram depicts epsilon/noise prediction. It also omits important details about the pretrained VQ-VAE and SDFusion initialization/training data, token-length handling, diffusion schedule, classifier-free conditioning if any, mesh preprocessing, category-wise synthetic counts, and baseline tuning. The promised release URL is blank in the submitted manuscript.

Baseline coverage is narrow and fairness is hard to verify. Only two main competitors are reported; one image baseline uses a materially different occupancy and super-resolution pipeline. There is no geometry-only transformer with matched capacity, no unordered-token version retaining stroke membership, and no retrieval or nearest-training-shape baseline to test whether the model generates input-specific geometry rather than selecting from a learned ShapeNet prior.

Evaluation is limited to aligned surface CD and F-score. Translation and scale alignment remove practically relevant errors, while no topology, diversity, part-structure, perceptual, or user-preference evaluation supports broader claims about design intent, interactive utility, or topology preservation. Qualitative results are selected examples, and the partial-sketch study does not establish that the inferred completion matches a user's intended shape.

Presentation issues are secondary but noticeable: the text conflates the 3DVRChair and proposed-dataset improvements in its discussion of Table 2, calls a transformer trained from scratch a BERT-style encoder without clearly separating architectural borrowing from pretraining, contains an erroneous DDIM citation year ('20121'), and makes first/open-source claims that cannot be verified from the anonymized, blank release link.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and relatively underexplored problem: generating 3D shapes from sequential VR sketches while preserving both stroke-level and point-level structure.

The proposed dataset is potentially valuable: it contains 20,838 synthetic pairs and 900 participant-drawn pairs spanning four object categories, substantially broadening the scale and category coverage of prior public VR-sketch resources.

The overall pipeline is coherent and practical. It combines a training-free synthetic-sketch generator, a lightweight sequence encoder, and an established latent 3D diffusion model, with reported training and inference costs.

The reported results are consistently favorable across the public 3DVRChair benchmark, the new dataset, few-shot adaptation, and partial-input experiments. The qualitative examples also show visibly better topology and detail than the illustrated Luo et al. baseline.

The ablations establish that synthetic pretraining, augmentation, and the proposed sequence representation are useful in the implemented system, even though they do not cleanly establish the paper's stronger causal claim about temporal order.
weaknesses: Material: The manuscript does not specify whether the ShapeNet objects underlying the synthetic training set, real fine-tuning set, and real test set are identity-disjoint. Because real sketches are drawn over ShapeNet models and synthetic sketches are generated from shapes, overlap could let the model learn the exact test geometries. Without explicit object-level split construction, the principal evaluation cannot establish generalization to unseen shapes.

Material: The central claim that temporal order matters is not adequately isolated. The 'w/o stroke ordering' ablation simultaneously removes stroke indices and within-stroke point indices, thereby discarding segmentation and local structural information as well as temporal order. The PointNet++ comparison also changes the entire encoder. A controlled permutation of stroke order and point order while retaining stroke membership is needed to distinguish temporal information from representation and architecture effects.

Material: The real-sketch benchmark is collected by having participants trace a visible reference mesh, after which every point is snapped onto that mesh. Its sketch-to-shape distance is consequently about ten times lower than that of 3DVRChair. This is closer to sparse surface annotation than unconstrained VR ideation, substantially limiting claims about realistic freehand input, design intent, and synthetic-to-real generalization.

Material: The synthetic ordering is produced by spatial-connectivity DFS, but the paper provides no evidence that this ordering resembles human drawing order. There are no sequence-statistics comparisons, human-order versus synthetic-order experiments, or tests on shuffled real sequences. This weakens the motivation for treating the generated sequences as supervision for human temporal behavior.

The empirical evidence is narrow relative to the claims: only two implemented baselines are reported, results on the new dataset are not broken down across all four categories, and there are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance analyses. For stochastic diffusion inference, the number of generated samples and whether metrics use one sample, an average, or selection among samples are also unspecified.

The completion experiment uses an artificial protocol—prefix truncation followed by learned MASK padding and randomly inserted SEP tokens—rather than genuinely interrupted user sketches. Since closely related masking augmentations are used during training, the strong robustness is partly expected, and the paper does not establish performance for other realistic missing-stroke patterns.

Several details needed for reproducibility are missing, including maximum sequence length and resampling/truncation policy, exact shape identities and split rules, validation and checkpoint-selection procedures, random seeds, diffusion guidance/sampling settings, VQ-VAE provenance and training categories, and sufficiently precise units or definitions for sketch-generation thresholds. The release URL is blank, despite repeated 'open-source' and 'open-access' claims.

There is a technical inconsistency in the diffusion description: the text says that the U-Net predicts a denoised latent and is trained against target latents, whereas Figure 3 depicts epsilon prediction. This should be resolved because it changes the stated training objective. Minor citation and typographical errors further reduce polish, but these are presentation issues rather than the basis for rejection.

Overall, the dataset and application have merit, but the unverified split integrity and confounded evidence for the paper's main 'order matters' claim are consequential. The current evidence therefore favors weak rejection rather than outright rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored problem: generating 3D shapes from temporally ordered VR strokes rather than treating sketches as unordered point clouds. The combined contribution of a sequential dataset, scalable synthetic-data pipeline, and order-aware generator is original and potentially useful for interactive 3D design.

The empirical results are consistently favorable. On 3DVRChair, the method improves F-score from 26.6 to 31.1 and reduces Chamfer distance from 35.5 to 25.8 relative to Luo et al.; on the new dataset, the gains are substantially larger across both chairs and all four categories.

The ablations provide direct evidence for important design choices: removing ordering lowers F-score from 56.8 to 48.9, removing augmentation yields 49.0, and replacing the encoder with a 3D SketchBERT variant yields 50.4. Point-cloud and multiview encodings perform considerably worse, supporting the sequential representation.

The evaluation includes an existing public benchmark, synthetic-to-real transfer, few-shot adaptation, partial-sketch completion, runtime measurements, quantitative metrics, and informative qualitative comparisons. This is broader support than a result confined to the authors' new benchmark.

The synthetic-sketch pipeline is pragmatic and scalable, producing 20,838 pairs in approximately ten hours, while the collection of 900 ordered real sketches across four categories materially expands the limited data available for this problem.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with effective pipeline diagrams and qualitative examples. The stated limitations concerning the frozen VQ-VAE and 64^3 SDF resolution are appropriate.
weaknesses: Material: The manuscript does not state whether reference shapes are disjoint across the synthetic training set, real fine-tuning set, and real evaluation set, or whether multiple sketches of the same ShapeNet model can cross splits. Because the model could learn shape-specific priors from synthetic versions of evaluation objects, explicit shape-level split construction is essential for interpreting the large results on the proposed benchmark.

Material: The real sketches are drawn over an existing target mesh and every point is projected onto that mesh by surface snapping. This produces unusually accurate traces—the reported sketch-to-shape distance is 5.5 versus 55.6 for 3DVRChair—but does not closely match deployment where the target shape is not already available. Consequently, results on this benchmark may overstate robustness to unconstrained VR sketches; the smaller gains on 3DVRChair are more persuasive.

Material: The partial-sketch experiment is not fully controlled. The proposed model is explicitly trained with stroke and point dropping, while comparable partial-input augmentation for the baseline is not reported. Random insertion of SEP tokens at inference also departs from simply preserving a genuine drawing prefix. Random-subset, reversed-order, and augmentation-matched controls would better establish that the advantage comes from temporal order and realistic completion behavior.

The ordering ablation removes both stroke-index and within-stroke point-index encodings simultaneously. It therefore establishes that positional structure helps, but does not isolate stroke order, point order, or stroke segmentation, nor compare against randomly permuted or reversed sequences. This limits the precision of the central 'order matters' conclusion.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: maximum sequence length, point resampling or truncation, padding and attention masking, category counts and source splits for synthetic shapes, exact pretrained VQ-VAE/SDFusion checkpoint and conditioning mechanism, and training hardware are not specified. The promised release link also appears blank in the submitted manuscript.

There is a technical-description inconsistency: the figure depicts epsilon/noise prediction, whereas the text says the U-Net minimizes reconstruction loss between predicted and target latents. The precise diffusion objective should be stated correctly. Results also lack multiple-seed variability or confidence intervals, and the qualitative evidence is limited to a small number of selected examples.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and underexplored problem: generating 3D shapes from temporally ordered VR sketches. The combination of a multi-category dataset, scalable synthetic-sketch generation, and an order-aware model is a meaningful contribution to sketch-based 3D vision.

The dataset is substantially broader than the cited public alternative: 20,838 synthetic pairs and 900 real sketches across four categories, with both point and stroke order retained. Collecting the real data from 15 participants and providing separate adaptation and evaluation subsets required appreciable effort.

The reported performance gains are large and consistent across the two evaluated datasets. On the proposed all-category benchmark, the method improves F-score from 48.8 to 69.8 and Chamfer distance from 13.0 to 4.8 relative to Luo et al.; it also improves both metrics on 3DVRChair.

The experiments examine several practically relevant dimensions, including zero/few-shot synthetic-to-real transfer, partial sketches, free-hand sketches, unseen categories, inference speed, and sketcher expertise. The matched ablations show that positional encoding, augmentation, and synthetic pretraining contribute materially.

The paper is generally clear, and the qualitative examples support the quantitative trend: the proposed method more often preserves thin structures, topology, and category-specific details than the displayed baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim that temporal drawing order matters is not cleanly established. The main "w/o ordering" ablation simultaneously removes stroke indices and within-stroke point indices, so it conflates temporal order with stroke membership, curve parameterization, and positional information. More importantly, Table A-1 shows that reversing stroke order has essentially no effect, scrambling strokes causes only a modest F-score reduction, and scrambling points changes Chamfer distance from 5.1 to only 5.2. These results support the usefulness of consistent sequence structure, but not the stronger framing that human temporal order or design intent is being recovered.

The manuscript does not state whether ShapeNet identities are disjoint across synthetic training, real fine-tuning, and real evaluation sets. Since real sketches are traced over ShapeNet reference models and synthetic sketches are also generated from shapes, shape-level overlap could allow the model to learn priors for evaluation objects rather than demonstrate transfer to unseen shapes. Explicit shape IDs, selection rules, and object-level split guarantees are necessary to interpret the main results.

The principal real benchmark is unusually clean: surface snapping projects every point onto the target object, and the reported sketch-to-shape distance is roughly ten times smaller than for 3DVRChair. This makes the input close to a sparse sample of the answer geometry. Robustness to unsnapped sketches is shown only qualitatively, while the free-hand study uses just 20 free-hand sketches and subjective ratings without corresponding ground-truth geometry. Thus, broad claims about realistic free-hand use are only weakly supported.

Baseline breadth and controlled comparison are limited. Only two prior systems are quantitatively compared, and LAS-Diffusion uses a substantially different 2D-view/occupancy representation. Although a PointNet++ variant is reported, the paper does not fully document whether generator capacity, optimization, token budget, and point sampling were matched. A same-backbone comparison among temporal encoding, stroke-set encoding, and order-invariant encoding would better isolate the claimed contribution.

Statistical support is insufficient. Results are reported without variation across training seeds or diffusion samples. The user study claims significant improvement but provides no statistical test, confidence interval over items, participant demographics, inter-rater analysis, or treatment of repeated ratings. It is also unclear whether diffusion evaluation uses one sample, an average, or best-of-multiple sampling.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the release claim: maximum sequence length, point resampling or truncation, category composition of the synthetic data, shape normalization, VQ-VAE pretraining, exact diffusion objective, conditioning mechanism, graph construction for DFS ordering, random-seed protocol, and baseline training details are not fully specified. The displayed open-source link is empty, so the claimed release cannot be verified from the submission.

There are smaller technical and presentation inconsistencies. The method description alternates between predicting a denoised latent and predicting epsilon, which leaves the diffusion loss ambiguous. Table A-2 labels increasing values as "samples/s" even though the text and main-paper timing indicate they are seconds per sample. Several typos and citation errors, including DDIM dated "20121," should be corrected. These issues are secondary to the experimental concerns above.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and relatively underexplored problem: generating 3D shapes from sequential VR sketches. Preserving stroke and point order is a sensible modeling direction, and the combination of a sequence encoder with latent 3D diffusion is technically coherent.

The dataset contribution is potentially valuable. It includes 20,838 synthetic pairs and 900 real sketches across four categories, substantially broadening the scale and category coverage of publicly described VR-sketch resources. The automatic sketch-generation pipeline could also reduce an important data-collection bottleneck.

The reported improvements are substantial on the proposed benchmark: the method reaches 69.8 F-score and 4.8 CD compared with 48.8 and 13.0 for Luo et al. The method also improves the public 3DVRChair benchmark, although by a smaller margin. Qualitative examples generally show more complete and faithful geometry than the baselines.

The experiments cover synthetic-to-real adaptation, representation alternatives, component ablations, partial sketches, free-hand inputs, unsnapped sketches, unseen categories, and inference speed. In particular, the strong failure without synthetic pretraining supports the practical utility of the proposed data-generation pipeline.
The manuscript is mostly clear, and the diagrams communicate the dataset pipeline and model architecture effectively.
weaknesses: The central claim that temporal order matters is not convincingly isolated. The main ablation removes both stroke-index and within-stroke point-index embeddings simultaneously. More importantly, the supplement shows that reversing the sequence has essentially no adverse effect (56.2 versus 56.8 F-score, with slightly better CD), while scrambling strokes causes only a modest reduction. These results support the weaker conclusion that consistent positional structure is a useful inductive bias, not the repeated claims that human drawing order encodes design intent or is intrinsically critical.

The principal benchmark is unusually favorable to reconstruction. Users trace visible reference shapes, and every point is snapped onto the ground-truth surface; predictions are subsequently translated and scaled to the ground truth for evaluation. This setting is substantially cleaner than early-stage VR ideation. Generalization to genuine free-hand input is evaluated on only 20 free-hand sketches through subjective ratings, without objective geometry measurements or a larger diverse test set.

The data splits are insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not state whether synthetic training shapes, real fine-tuning shapes, and real test shapes are disjoint at the underlying ShapeNet-model level, nor whether participants are separated across splits. Because the synthetic data and reference-guided real sketches can derive from the same shape collection, shape-identity overlap could materially inflate the reported synthetic-to-real results. This is a consequential reproducibility and validity concern rather than a presentation refinement.

The comparisons do not cleanly establish that ordering explains the large gain. The point-cloud and multiview alternatives change the encoder, sampling, rendering, and sometimes output representation or super-resolution pipeline in addition to discarding order. A stronger control would use the same-capacity encoder and generator with shuffled sequences, consistently randomized order during training and testing, or order-invariant pooling. The supplementary perturbations help but also weaken the headline claim.

Statistical support is limited. Results are reported without variation over training seeds or confidence intervals, and the claimed significance of the user study is unsupported by a stated statistical test. Treating 1,900 repeated ratings as independent would also overstate the effective sample size because they cover only 40 sketches and 38 raters.

Several implementation details needed for reproduction are missing or ambiguous, including shape-level split construction, sequence resampling and maximum length, handling of longer sketches, the exact pretrained VQ-VAE checkpoint, and participant distribution across samples. The promised open-source link is blank in the submitted manuscript.

Some numerical and reporting issues need correction: Table A-2 labels latency values as samples per second even though larger values correspond to more DDIM steps and the text describes them as seconds per sketch; 2.26 to 6.33 seconds is slightly less than a threefold difference despite the claim of over 3×; and the paper alternates between 6.61 and 6.33 seconds for the 100-step setting. These are presentation-level issues, but they reduce confidence in the experimental reporting.

Overall, the dataset and empirical results are promising, but the unclear possibility of shape leakage, evaluation on surface-snapped traces, and mismatch between the evidence and the headline temporal-order claim leave the paper near the acceptance boundary rather than supporting a clear accept.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored problem: generating 3D shapes from sequential VR sketches while retaining stroke and point structure. The combination of dataset construction, synthetic-data generation, and a sketch-conditioned generator constitutes a substantial contribution.

The dataset is valuable in scale and breadth: 20,838 synthetic pairs and 900 real sketch–shape pairs across four categories, compared with the single-category 3DVRChair benchmark. Preserving stroke and point indices should support research beyond the proposed model.

The reported quantitative gains are strong. On the new four-category benchmark, the method reaches 69.8 F-score and 4.8 CD, versus 48.8 and 13.0 for the strongest baseline. It also improves over prior methods on the independent 3DVRChair benchmark, reducing concern that the gains arise only from the new collection protocol.

The ablations provide useful evidence for several components: removing sequence indices reduces zero-shot chair performance from 56.8 to 48.9 F-score, removing augmentation gives 49.0, and replacing the encoder with PointNet++ gives 30.8. Additional perturbation experiments and partial-sketch evaluation further probe the sequential representation.

Synthetic-to-real transfer is practically encouraging. The model reportedly works zero-shot, approaches its best performance with roughly 50 real examples per category, and remains effective on partial inputs. The user study also favors the method for both reference-guided and free-hand sketches.

The method is technically coherent and clearly described: Fourier coordinate features, separate stroke/point indices, a lightweight transformer, and latent SDF diffusion form a sensible architecture. Runtime and sampling-step tradeoffs are reported, and the qualitative results generally support the numerical findings.
weaknesses: The central claim about temporal drawing order is only partially isolated. The main “without ordering” ablation simultaneously removes stroke identity and within-stroke point position, so it conflates temporal order with polyline grouping and local curve parameterization. Reversing the stroke order has almost no effect (56.8 versus 56.2 F-score), while scrambling strokes causes only a modest decline. The evidence therefore supports structured sequential encoding more strongly than it supports the broader claim that human drawing order or design intent is essential.

The manuscript does not clearly state whether ShapeNet identities are disjoint across synthetic pretraining, real fine-tuning, and real testing. Because real sketches are traced over reference ShapeNet objects, synthetic training sketches generated from the same meshes would create target-shape leakage even if the sketches themselves differ. A precise shape-level split protocol is necessary to establish the validity and reproducibility of the main benchmark.

Most real benchmark sketches are surface-snapped to visible reference objects, making them unusually well aligned with their targets and less representative of unconstrained ideation. Robustness to unsnapped and unseen-category sketches is shown only qualitatively, while the free-hand study contains just 20 free-hand sketches. These results are promising but do not fully substantiate broad real-world generalization.

The user-study claim of significant improvement is not supported by a reported statistical test, confidence interval for the paired difference, or analysis accounting for repeated ratings by participants and items. The study also does not explain how its 40 generated examples were selected, which limits the strength of this evidence.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the release claim: the paper omits maximum sequence length and sequence resampling/truncation rules, exact SDFusion/VQ-VAE initialization and training provenance, sampling seeds or aggregation for stochastic predictions, and a sufficiently precise construction of the train/test shape splits. Table A-2 also labels its increasing runtime values as “samples/s,” although they appear to be seconds per sample.

Baseline coverage is relatively narrow, and some headline percentage statements do not match the corresponding 3DVRChair numbers. For example, Table 2 shows improvements from 26.6 to 31.1 F-score and from 35.5 to 25.8 CD on 3DVRChair, not the stated over-40% F-score gain and over-60% CD reduction. This is a correctable reporting issue rather than a fundamental flaw.
